title.en: Introduction to Database System and SQL Commands

body.en:
Data are raw, unorganised facts and figures (numbers, text, images, sound) that have no meaning by themselves. Example: 82, Aarav, Surat, CE.

Information is data that has been processed (organised, classified, calculated) so that it is meaningful and useful for decision making. Example: "Aarav of CE scored 82 marks and stood 2nd in the class."

Processing steps: collecting → recording → classifying → sorting → calculating → summarising → reporting.

Difference between data and information

DataInformation
Raw factsProcessed data
UnorganisedOrganised and structured
No meaning aloneMeaningful in a context
Input to processingOutput of processing
Not useful for decisionsHelps in decision making
Example: 35, 42, 28Average temperature = 35 °C

The information produced by one process can become the data for another process (e.g. the marks of each subject → total → class rank).

Qualities of good information: accurate, complete, timely, relevant, easy to understand and cost-effective.

h.en: Data Item, Record, File and Database

body.en:
Data in a database are organised in a hierarchy, from the smallest unit to the largest:

  1. Data item (field / attribute / column): the smallest named unit of data that has meaning. Example: NAME = 'Diya Shah'. A data item has a name, a type and a size.
  2. Record (tuple / row): a collection of related data items about one entity (one student, one employee). Example: (2, 'Diya Shah', 'IT', 91).
  3. File (table / relation): a collection of records of the same type. Example: the STUDENT file holds the records of all students.
  4. Database: a collection of logically related files. Example: a college database has STUDENT, FACULTY, COURSE and RESULT files.

Other terms:

  • Entity: a real-world object about which data is stored (student, book, account).
  • Key field: a field whose value uniquely identifies each record (roll number, account number).
  • In relational terms: table = relation, row = tuple, column = attribute, number of columns = degree, number of rows = cardinality.

Metadata means "data about data". It describes the data instead of being the data itself: table names, column names, data types, sizes, constraints, indexes, owners, privileges, creation date, etc.

Example: "NAME is VARCHAR2(15) and NOT NULL" is metadata; "Diya Shah" is data.

The data dictionary (system catalog) is a set of special tables in which the DBMS stores all the metadata of the database. It is created and updated automatically by the DBMS whenever a DDL command (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) runs. Users can only read it.

Contents of the data dictionary

  • Names and structure of all tables, views, indexes, sequences and synonyms
  • Column names, data types, sizes and default values
  • Integrity constraints (primary key, foreign key, check ...)
  • Users, roles and their privileges
  • Storage and audit information

Types

  • Active (integrated): managed by the DBMS itself and updated automatically. Oracle's dictionary is active.
  • Passive (non-integrated): kept separately (e.g. as documents) and updated manually.

In Oracle the dictionary is read through views such as USER_TABLES, USER_TAB_COLUMNS, USER_CONSTRAINTS, ALL_TABLES and DBA_USERS. The DESC command also reads it.

SELECT table_name
FROM user_tables;

SELECT column_name, data_type
FROM user_tab_columns
WHERE table_name = 'STUDENT';

Uses: the DBMS checks every query against it (does the table exist? does the user have the privilege?), and it documents the database for DBAs and developers.

Database: a shared, integrated collection of logically related data, stored with minimum redundancy, that serves the needs of many users. Example: a bank database (customers, accounts, transactions).

DBMS (Database Management System): software that is used to create, store, retrieve, update and manage a database. It acts as an interface between the users/application programs and the database. Examples: Oracle, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, PostgreSQL, IBM DB2, MS Access.

Database system = database + DBMS software + application programs + users.

RDBMS (Relational DBMS): a DBMS based on the relational model of E. F. Codd (1970). The data is stored in tables (relations) of rows and columns, and the tables are related through common columns (keys). SQL is used to work with the data. Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL are RDBMSs.

Functions / characteristics of a DBMS

  • Data definition: creates the structure (tables) using DDL
  • Data manipulation: insert, update, delete and query data
  • Data storage management and the data dictionary
  • Security: users, passwords and privileges
  • Integrity: constraints keep the data correct
  • Concurrency control: many users at the same time
  • Backup and recovery after failures
  • Transaction management (ACID)

DBMS vs RDBMS

DBMSRDBMS
Data may be stored as files, hierarchy or networkData stored in related tables
Relationships are not enforcedKeys enforce relationships
Normalization not requiredNormalization supported
Usually single user, small dataMulti-user, large data
Example: file systems, XML storesOracle, MySQL, SQL Server

h.en: File Processing System vs Database System

body.en:
Before DBMSs, each department kept its own data files and wrote its own programs to process them (the file processing system). This approach has many problems.

Disadvantages of the file processing system

  1. Data redundancy: the same data (student name, address) is stored in many files, wasting space.
  2. Data inconsistency: when one copy is updated and another is not, the copies disagree.
  3. Difficult data access: a new program must be written for every new query.
  4. Data isolation: data are scattered in files of different formats.
  5. Integrity problems: rules (e.g. marks ≤ 100) are hidden inside program code and are hard to change.
  6. Atomicity problems: after a crash in the middle of an update, the data is left half-changed.
  7. Concurrent access anomalies: two users updating together can corrupt the data.
  8. Security problems: it is hard to give each user access to only part of the data.

Advantages of a DBMS

  • Controlled redundancy and better consistency
  • Data sharing among many users and applications
  • Integrity constraints enforced centrally
  • Security through users, roles and privileges
  • Backup and recovery, and transaction support
  • Easy querying with SQL; data independence
  • Standards can be enforced

Disadvantages of a DBMS

  • High cost of software, hardware and trained staff
  • Complex to design and manage; needs a DBA
  • A failure of the central database affects all users
  • Extra overhead, so it is slower than files for very small, simple jobs

• Banking: customer accounts, loans, ATM and UPI transactions
  • Railway and airline reservation: IRCTC bookings, seat availability, schedules
  • Universities: student registration, GTU exam results, fees
  • Telecom: call records, prepaid balance, monthly bills
  • E-commerce: products, orders and payments (Amazon, Flipkart)
  • Hospitals: patient records, doctors, billing
  • Government: Aadhaar, income tax, voter lists
  • HR and payroll: employee details, attendance, salaries
  • Social media: profiles, posts, messages

A database system has five main components:

  1. Hardware: computers, storage disks, servers and network devices on which the database runs.
  2. Software: the DBMS itself, the operating system, network software and application programs.
  3. Data: the stored database (user data) and the metadata in the data dictionary.
  4. Procedures: rules and instructions for using and managing the system (login, backup, recovery steps).
  5. Users (people): everyone who interacts with the database.

Main parts of the DBMS software

  • Query processor: DDL interpreter, DML compiler and query optimiser. It checks a query, chooses the best plan and runs it.
  • Storage manager: file manager, buffer manager, authorisation and integrity manager. It moves data between disk and memory.
  • Transaction manager: ensures ACID properties, concurrency control (locking) and recovery.
  • Data dictionary: stores the metadata used by all the other parts.

Types of database users

  1. Naive (end) users: use ready-made application screens without knowing SQL. Example: a bank clerk or an ATM user.
  2. Application programmers: write programs (Java, Python, PHP) that use the database through SQL.
  3. Sophisticated / casual users: analysts who write their own SQL queries or use reporting tools.
  4. Specialised users: write special database applications (CAD, expert systems).
  5. Database Administrator (DBA): the person with central control over the database.

Responsibilities of the DBA

  • Schema definition: designs and creates the database structure
  • Storage structure and access method definition (tablespaces, indexes)
  • Creating users and granting/revoking privileges (security)
  • Defining integrity constraints
  • Regular backup and recovery after failures
  • Monitoring and tuning performance
  • Installing and upgrading the DBMS software

The ANSI/SPARC architecture separates the user's view of the database from the way the data is physically stored. It has three levels:

  1. External level (view level): the highest level. Each user or group sees only the part of the database they need (a view). Example: the exam cell sees roll no., name and marks but not fees. There can be many external views.
  2. Conceptual level (logical level): describes the whole database for the community of users: all tables, columns, data types, relationships and constraints, without storage details. There is only one conceptual schema. It is designed by the DBA.
  3. Internal level (physical level): the lowest level. It describes how the data is actually stored on disk: file organisation, record layout, indexes, compression and access paths.

Mappings connect the levels: external/conceptual mapping and conceptual/internal mapping. The DBMS uses them to convert a user's request into operations on the stored data.

Data independence

The ability to change the schema at one level without changing the schema at the next higher level.

  • Logical data independence: the conceptual schema can be changed (e.g. a new column or table is added) without changing the external views or application programs.
  • Physical data independence: the internal schema can be changed (e.g. a new index, a different disk, a new file organisation) without changing the conceptual schema.

Physical data independence is easier to achieve than logical data independence.

Objectives of the three-level architecture

  • Each user can see the data in their own way.
  • Users need not know storage details.
  • The DBA can change storage without affecting users.
  • It provides data independence and security.

• 1-tier: the user, the application and the database are all on the same machine. Example: a student using Oracle SQL*Plus on a laptop to practise.
  • 2-tier (client-server): the client machine runs the application (user interface and logic); it talks directly to the database server using ODBC/JDBC. Example: a desktop billing application in a shop connected to a database server. It is simple, but it is difficult to scale and less secure.
  • 3-tier: the client (browser) → the application server (business logic, e.g. Java, PHP, Node.js) → the database server. The client never accesses the database directly. Used by web applications such as IRCTC and online banking. It is scalable, secure and easier to maintain.
2-tier3-tier
Client talks to the DB directlyClient → app server → DB
Business logic on the clientBusiness logic on the app server
Fewer users, less secureMany users, more secure
Desktop LAN applicationsWeb applications

Schema: the overall logical structure (design) of the database: table names, column names, data types, keys, relationships and constraints. It is defined with DDL during design and changes rarely. It is like the plan of a building or a class in programming.

Example schema: STUDENT(rollno, name, branch, city, marks)

By level there are three schemas: the external schema (views), the conceptual (logical) schema and the internal (physical) schema.

Sub-schema: a subset of the schema that is visible to a particular user or application. It hides the rest of the data and gives security and simplicity. In SQL a sub-schema is created using a view. Example: the exam cell's sub-schema (rollno, name, marks); the accounts section's sub-schema (rollno, name, fees).

Instance (database state / snapshot): the actual data stored in the database at a particular moment. Every INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE creates a new instance. The schema stays the same.

Schema vs Instance

SchemaInstance
Structure / design of the DBData in the DB at one moment
Defined using DDLChanged using DML
Changes rarelyChanges frequently
Like a class / blueprintLike objects / a snapshot
Called the intensionCalled the extension

SQL (Structured Query Language), pronounced "sequel", is the standard language used to create, manage and query relational databases. It was developed by IBM in the 1970s (as SEQUEL for System R) and is standardised by ANSI and ISO.

Features of SQL

  • Non-procedural: you say what data you want, not how to get it.
  • English-like, easy to learn commands (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ...)
  • One language for defining, manipulating, querying and controlling data
  • Portable: works on Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server, PostgreSQL (with small differences)
  • Can be embedded in programs (Java, Python, C) and extended with PL/SQL

Rules for writing SQL statements

  • Keywords are not case-sensitive: SELECT = select. But data inside quotes is case-sensitive.
  • A statement can span many lines and ends with a semicolon ; in SQL*Plus.
  • Text and date values are written in single quotes: 'Surat'.
  • Names (tables, columns) start with a letter, can have up to 30 characters (128 in Oracle 12.2+), and may contain letters, digits, _, $ and #.
  • Comments: -- single line and /* multi line */.

Oracle tools: SQL*Plus (command line), SQL Developer (GUI) and Oracle Live SQL (online).

Every column must have a data type, which decides what kind of values it can hold and how much space they take.

Character types

  • CHAR(n): fixed-length text of n characters (max 2000 bytes). Shorter values are padded with spaces. Use for fixed codes: gender 'M'/'F', state code 'GJ'.
  • VARCHAR2(n): variable-length text of up to n characters (max 4000 bytes; 32767 with extended size). It stores only the actual characters, so there is no wasted space. This is the most used text type.
  • VARCHAR(n): currently the same as VARCHAR2, but reserved by Oracle for future use, so use VARCHAR2.
  • NCHAR / NVARCHAR2: Unicode text (for Gujarati, Hindi and other languages).
  • LONG: variable text up to 2 GB (old type; only one per table; use CLOB instead).

Number type

  • NUMBER(p, s): p = precision (total digits, 1 to 38), s = scale (digits after the decimal point). NUMBER(7,2) stores up to 99999.99.
  • NUMBER(5) = whole numbers up to 5 digits. NUMBER alone = any number (floating).
  • INTEGER, INT, SMALLINT, DECIMAL and FLOAT are accepted and mapped to NUMBER.

Date and time types

  • DATE: stores the date and time (century, year, month, day, hour, minute, second). The default display is DD-MON-YY, e.g. 28-OCT-26.
  • TIMESTAMP: date and time with fractions of a second.
  • INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH / DAY TO SECOND: a period of time.

Large object (LOB) and binary types

  • CLOB: large text (up to 128 TB), e.g. articles and descriptions.
  • BLOB: large binary data such as images, audio and video.
  • BFILE: a pointer to a binary file stored outside the database.
  • RAW(n) / LONG RAW: small/large binary data.

Others: ROWID (the physical address of a row) and BOOLEAN (only in PL/SQL before 23ai).

CREATE TABLE product (
  pid    NUMBER(5),
  pname  VARCHAR2(30),
  grade  CHAR(1),
  price  NUMBER(8,2),
  mfg_dt DATE,
  photo  BLOB
);

CHAR vs VARCHAR2

CHAR(n)VARCHAR2(n)
Fixed lengthVariable length
Pads with spacesNo padding
Max 2000 bytesMax 4000 bytes
Wastes space for short valuesSaves space
Slightly faster for fixed dataBest for names, addresses
'GJ' in CHAR(5) = 'GJ ''GJ' in VARCHAR2(5) = 'GJ'

title.en: 1.5 SQL Commands: DDL, DML and DQL

body.en:
SQL commands are divided into five groups according to their purpose:

GroupPurposeCommands
DDL Data Definition LanguageCreate/change/remove the structure of objectsCREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME
DML Data Manipulation LanguageAdd, change, remove rowsINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
DQL Data Query LanguageRetrieve dataSELECT
DCL Data Control LanguageGive/take privilegesGRANT, REVOKE
TCL Transaction Control LanguageManage transactionsCOMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT

Note: DDL and DCL commands are auto-committed in Oracle; DML changes stay temporary until COMMIT.

h.en: DDL: CREATE DATABASE and CREATE TABLE

body.en:
CREATE DATABASE creates a new, empty database. In MySQL/SQL Server it is used often. In Oracle, the database is created once by the DBA (using the DBCA tool or the CREATE DATABASE statement), and each user works in their own schema inside it.

CREATE DATABASE college;   -- MySQL style

-- Oracle: a database is created once by
-- the DBA (DBCA tool); users then create
-- schemas (users) and tables in it.
CREATE USER college IDENTIFIED BY pwd;

CREATE TABLE creates a new table: its name, its columns with data types and sizes, and optional constraints.

CREATE TABLE table_name (
  column1 datatype [constraint],
  column2 datatype [constraint],
  ...
  [table_constraints]
);
  • A table name must be unique in the schema and must not be a reserved word.
  • Each column needs a name and a data type; the size is given in brackets.
  • Constraints (PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL ...) can be written with a column or at the end (studied in Unit 4).
  • DESC table_name shows the structure of the table.
  • A table can also be created from another table: CREATE TABLE new AS SELECT ...

ALTER TABLE changes the structure of an existing table without losing its data.

ALTER TABLE t ADD (col datatype, ...);
ALTER TABLE t MODIFY (col new_datatype);
ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN col;
ALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN old TO new;
ALTER TABLE t RENAME TO new_name;
RENAME old_name TO new_name;
  • ADD: adds one or more new columns (at the end). Old rows get NULL in them.
  • MODIFY: changes the data type or size of a column. Size can be decreased, or the type changed, only if the existing data fits.
  • DROP COLUMN: removes a column and its data.
  • RENAME COLUMN: changes a column name.
  • RENAME TO / RENAME: changes the table name.
  • ALTER is also used to add or drop constraints: ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT ...

DROP TABLE table_name;
DROP TABLE table_name PURGE;
TRUNCATE TABLE table_name;
  • DROP TABLE removes the whole table: its structure, data, indexes and constraints. In Oracle 10g+ it goes to the recycle bin (PURGE removes it permanently).
  • TRUNCATE TABLE removes all rows quickly but keeps the structure. Storage is released and it cannot be rolled back.

DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP

DELETETRUNCATEDROP
DMLDDLDDL
Removes selected rows (WHERE allowed)Removes all rowsRemoves rows + structure
Can be rolled backCannot be rolled backCannot be rolled back (Flashback possible)
Slow: logs every rowFastFast
Fires DELETE triggersNo triggersNo triggers
Structure staysStructure staysTable no longer exists

INSERT adds new rows to a table.

INSERT INTO t VALUES (v1, v2, ...);

INSERT INTO t (col1, col2)
VALUES (v1, v2);

INSERT INTO t (col1, col2)
SELECT c1, c2 FROM other WHERE ...;
  • Without a column list, values must be given for all columns in table order.
  • With a column list, unlisted columns get NULL (or their DEFAULT value).
  • Strings and dates are enclosed in single quotes. A date can be written as '15-AUG-2024' or with TO_DATE('15-08-2024','DD-MM-YYYY').
  • Substitution variables (&var) make SQL*Plus ask for values, so many rows can be inserted with one statement (run again with /).
  • INSERT INTO ... SELECT copies rows from another table.

UPDATE modifies the values of existing rows.

UPDATE table_name
SET col1 = value1, col2 = value2
[WHERE condition];
  • SET gives the new values; more than one column can be changed at a time.
  • The new value can be an expression using the old value: SET sal = sal * 1.10.
  • WHERE selects the rows to change. If WHERE is omitted, all rows are updated.
  • Oracle reports how many rows were updated.

DELETE removes rows from a table.

DELETE FROM table_name
[WHERE condition];
  • Only the rows satisfying WHERE are removed; without WHERE all rows are deleted, but the table remains.
  • A whole row is deleted; to clear only one column, use UPDATE ... SET col = NULL.
  • DELETE can be undone by ROLLBACK until COMMIT.

SELECT retrieves data from one or more tables. It never changes data. Full form:

SELECT [DISTINCT] col1 [AS alias], ...
FROM table_name
[WHERE condition]
[GROUP BY columns]
[HAVING group_condition]
[ORDER BY columns [ASC|DESC]];
  • SELECT * shows all columns; otherwise list the required columns.
  • Expressions (sal * 12) are calculated for each row in the output only.
  • Column alias: expr AS name or expr "Any Name" sets the heading.
  • WHERE filters rows using comparison operators (=, <> or !=, >, <, >=, <=) and logical operators (AND, OR, NOT).
  • DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result.
  • The order of execution is: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY.

Operators, functions, ORDER BY, GROUP BY and joins are covered in Unit 2.

title.en: 1.6 DCL: Users, Roles, GRANT and REVOKE

body.en:
Every person who connects to Oracle needs a user account (username + password). In Oracle, each user also owns a schema: the set of objects (tables, views ...) created by that user. Users are created by the DBA (SYS/SYSTEM).

CREATE USER username
  IDENTIFIED BY password;
ALTER USER username
  IDENTIFIED BY new_password;
DROP USER username CASCADE;
  • A new user cannot even log in until given the CREATE SESSION privilege.
  • DROP USER ... CASCADE also drops all objects owned by the user.
  • A user accesses another user's table as owner.table, e.g. scott.emp.

A privilege is the right to run a particular SQL statement or to access an object.

  • System privileges: the right to perform an action in the database: CREATE SESSION, CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, CREATE USER, DROP ANY TABLE ...
  • Object privileges: the right to perform an action on a specific object: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, ALTER, INDEX, REFERENCES on a table; EXECUTE on a procedure.

A role is a named group of related privileges that can be granted to users. When privileges change, only the role is changed and all its users get the change. Predefined roles: CONNECT, RESOURCE, DBA.

CREATE ROLE role_name;
GRANT privileges ON table TO role_name;
GRANT role_name TO user1, user2;
REVOKE role_name FROM user1;
DROP ROLE role_name;

Advantages of roles

  • Easy privilege management for many users
  • Dynamic: changing the role affects all its users
  • Can be enabled/disabled and protected with a password

GRANT gives privileges to users or roles.

GRANT privilege_list
ON object_name
TO user | role | PUBLIC
[WITH GRANT OPTION];

GRANT system_privilege TO user;
  • ALL grants all object privileges; PUBLIC means every user.
  • WITH GRANT OPTION: the receiver can grant the same privilege to others (for object privileges). For system privileges use WITH ADMIN OPTION.
  • UPDATE can be limited to columns: GRANT UPDATE (marks) ON student TO ravi;

REVOKE takes back privileges that were granted.

REVOKE privilege_list
ON object_name
FROM user | role | PUBLIC;
  • Only the grantor (or the DBA) can revoke.
  • Revoking an object privilege that was given WITH GRANT OPTION also removes it from the users to whom it was passed on (cascading).

title.en: 1.7 TCL: Transactions, ACID, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT

body.en:
A transaction is a logical unit of work that contains one or more SQL statements and must be completed fully or not at all. Example: transferring money is one transaction of two updates.

UPDATE account SET bal = bal - 500
WHERE acno = 'A';
UPDATE account SET bal = bal + 500
WHERE acno = 'B';
COMMIT;

If the system fails after the first UPDATE, Rs 500 would vanish. The DBMS prevents this by guaranteeing the ACID properties:

  1. Atomicity: all operations of the transaction are done, or none are. If any part fails, everything is rolled back. (Handled by the transaction/recovery manager using undo logs.)
  2. Consistency: a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state. All constraints remain true (the total of A + B stays the same).
  3. Isolation: concurrently running transactions do not see each other's uncommitted changes; the result is as if they ran one after another. (Handled by concurrency control/locking.)
  4. Durability: once a transaction is committed, its changes are permanent and survive power failures or crashes. (Handled by redo logs and backups.)

In Oracle, a transaction starts with the first DML statement and ends with COMMIT, ROLLBACK, a DDL/DCL statement (auto-commit) or the end of the session.

1. Active: the initial state; the statements are being executed.
  2. Partially committed: the last statement has been executed, but the changes are still in memory buffers.
  3. Committed: the changes are written permanently to the database after successful completion.
  4. Failed: normal execution cannot continue (error, constraint violation, system crash).
  5. Aborted: the transaction is rolled back and the database is restored to its state before the transaction. It may then be restarted or killed.

Committed and aborted are the terminated states.

COMMIT [WORK];
ROLLBACK [WORK];
SAVEPOINT savepoint_name;
ROLLBACK TO [SAVEPOINT] savepoint_name;
  • COMMIT: ends the current transaction and makes all its changes permanent and visible to other users. Locks are released and savepoints are erased.
  • ROLLBACK: ends the current transaction and undoes all changes made since the last COMMIT.
  • Implicit (automatic) COMMIT happens when a DDL or DCL statement runs or on a normal exit from SQL*Plus. SET AUTOCOMMIT ON commits after every DML statement.
  • Implicit ROLLBACK happens on an abnormal end of the session or a system failure.
  • Before COMMIT, other users still see the old data, and the changed rows are locked.

A SAVEPOINT is a named marker inside a transaction. It divides a long transaction into smaller parts so that you can undo only a part of it.

  • SAVEPOINT name; creates the marker.
  • ROLLBACK TO name; undoes only the changes made after that savepoint. The transaction is still active; earlier changes are kept (not yet committed).
  • Savepoints after the one rolled back to are erased; the named savepoint itself remains.
  • Creating a savepoint with an existing name moves it to the new position.
  • COMMIT or a plain ROLLBACK erases all savepoints.

title.en: Create a table and view its structure (CREATE, DESC)

code.en:
CREATE TABLE student (
  rollno NUMBER(3) PRIMARY KEY,
  name   VARCHAR2(15) NOT NULL,
  branch VARCHAR2(5),
  city   VARCHAR2(10),
  marks  NUMBER(3)
);

DESC student

programs.out:
Table created.

 Name    Null?    Type
 ------- -------- ------------
 ROLLNO  NOT NULL NUMBER(3)
 NAME    NOT NULL VARCHAR2(15)
 BRANCH           VARCHAR2(5)
 CITY             VARCHAR2(10)
 MARKS            NUMBER(3)

expl.en:
CREATE TABLE defines a new table: its name, each column's name and data type, and optional constraints.

  • NUMBER(3) holds whole numbers of up to 3 digits; VARCHAR2(15) holds text of up to 15 characters.
  • PRIMARY KEY makes rollno unique and not null, so it shows NOT NULL in DESC.
  • DESC (DESCRIBE) is a SQL*Plus command that shows column names, the Null? flag and the data types. It reads the data dictionary.

DESC is not an SQL statement, so it does not need a semicolon.

title.en: Table using different Oracle data types

code.en:
CREATE TABLE employee (
  emp_id   NUMBER(4),
  emp_name VARCHAR2(20),
  gender   CHAR(1),
  salary   NUMBER(8,2),
  join_dt  DATE,
  resume   CLOB
);

DESC employee

programs.out:
Table created.

 Name      Null?    Type
 --------- -------- ------------
 EMP_ID             NUMBER(4)
 EMP_NAME           VARCHAR2(20)
 GENDER             CHAR(1)
 SALARY             NUMBER(8,2)
 JOIN_DT            DATE
 RESUME             CLOB

expl.en:
• CHAR(1): fixed length. 'M' is stored as exactly 1 character (blank-padded if shorter).
  • NUMBER(8,2): precision 8 and scale 2, so 6 digits before the decimal point and 2 after (max 999999.99).
  • DATE: stores the date and time (century, year, month, day, hour, minute, second).
  • CLOB: a large text object (up to GBs), e.g. a resume or description.

No constraints are given, so every column is nullable (the Null? column is empty).

title.en: ALTER TABLE: add new columns and modify a column

programs.out:
Table altered.

Table altered.

 Name    Null?    Type
 ------- -------- ------------
 ROLLNO  NOT NULL NUMBER(3)
 NAME    NOT NULL VARCHAR2(15)
 BRANCH           VARCHAR2(5)
 CITY             VARCHAR2(20)
 MARKS            NUMBER(3)
 EMAIL            VARCHAR2(30)
 PHONE            NUMBER(10)

expl.en:
• ADD appends new columns at the end of the table. Existing rows get NULL in the new columns.
  • MODIFY changes a column's data type or size. Here city grows from VARCHAR2(10) to VARCHAR2(20).
  • Decreasing a size or changing a type is allowed only if the existing data fits (or the column is empty).

title.en: ALTER TABLE: drop and rename a column, rename the table

programs.out:
Table altered.

Table altered.

Table renamed.

 Name    Null?    Type
 ------- -------- ------------
 ROLLNO  NOT NULL NUMBER(3)
 NAME    NOT NULL VARCHAR2(15)
 BRANCH           VARCHAR2(5)
 TOTAL            NUMBER(3)

expl.en:
• DROP COLUMN removes the column and all its data permanently.
  • RENAME COLUMN old TO new changes only the column name; the data stays.
  • RENAME old TO new renames the table itself. ALTER TABLE student RENAME TO stud; does the same.

programs.out:
COUNT(*)
--------
       5

Table truncated.

no rows selected

 Name    Null?    Type
 ------- -------- ------------
 ROLLNO  NOT NULL NUMBER(3)

Table dropped.

ERROR at line 1:
ORA-00942: table or view does not exist

expl.en:
• TRUNCATE deletes all rows but keeps the table structure, so DESC still works and SELECT says "no rows selected".
  • DROP removes the rows and the structure. After that, the table does not exist: ORA-00942.
  • Both are DDL: they auto-commit and cannot be undone with ROLLBACK. (Oracle 10g+ keeps dropped tables in the Recycle Bin: FLASHBACK TABLE student TO BEFORE DROP;)

title.en: INSERT rows: all columns, selected columns, NULL

programs.out:
1 row created.

1 row created.

1 row created.

ROLLNO NAME        BRANCH CITY  MARKS
------ ----------- ------ ----- -----
     1 Aarav Patel CE     Surat    82
     2 Diya Shah   IT
     3 Karan Mehta CE              67

expl.en:
• Form 1: values for all columns, in the same order as the table.
  • Form 2: a column list. The missing columns (city, marks) get NULL.
  • Form 3: NULL written explicitly.
  • Text and date values go in single quotes; numbers do not.

NULL means "unknown / not given". It shows as a blank in the output.

title.en: Insert many rows with substitution variables (&)

programs.out:
Enter value for rollno: 6
Enter value for name: Meera Iyer
Enter value for branch: IT
Enter value for city: Navsari
Enter value for marks: 88
old   2: (&rollno, '&name', '&branch',
new   2: (6, 'Meera Iyer', 'IT',
old   3:  '&city', &marks)
new   3:  'Navsari', 88)

1 row created.

SQL> /
Enter value for rollno: 7
Enter value for name: Jay Trivedi
Enter value for branch: CE
Enter value for city: Anand
Enter value for marks: 79
old   2: (&rollno, '&name', '&branch',
new   2: (7, 'Jay Trivedi', 'CE',
old   3:  '&city', &marks)
new   3:  'Anand', 79)

1 row created.

expl.en:
In SQL*Plus, &name is a substitution variable. SQL*Plus asks for each value at run time, so one INSERT can be reused for many rows.

  • After the first row, type / and press Enter to run the same INSERT again for the next row.
  • Text variables are written inside quotes ('&name'), so the user does not have to type the quotes.
  • The old/new lines show the statement before and after substitution (turn them off with SET VERIFY OFF).

programs.out:
3 rows updated.

1 row updated.

ROLLNO NAME        CITY      MARKS
------ ----------- --------- -----
     1 Aarav Patel Surat        87
     2 Diya Shah   Ahmedabad    95
     3 Karan Mehta Rajkot       72
     4 Isha Desai  Surat        74
     5 Rohan Joshi Bharuch      63

expl.en:
• UPDATE changes values in existing rows. WHERE chooses which rows are changed.
  • The first UPDATE adds 5 marks to every CE student (3 rows). An expression can use the old value (marks + 5).
  • Several columns can be set at once, separated by commas.
  • Without WHERE, all rows are updated. Always check the WHERE clause first.

programs.out:
1 row deleted.

0 rows deleted.

ROLLNO NAME        MARKS
------ ----------- -----
     1 Aarav Patel    82
     2 Diya Shah      91
     3 Karan Mehta    67
     4 Isha Desai     74

expl.en:
• DELETE removes whole rows that satisfy the WHERE condition (Rohan, 58 marks).
  • If no row matches, Oracle reports 0 rows deleted. This is not an error.
  • DELETE FROM student; without WHERE deletes every row, but unlike TRUNCATE it can be rolled back because DELETE is DML.

title.en: Copy a table (CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT, INSERT ... SELECT)

programs.out:
Table created.

ROLLNO NAME        MARKS
------ ----------- -----

1 row created.

ROLLNO NAME        MARKS
------ ----------- -----
     1 Aarav Patel    82
     3 Karan Mehta    67
     5 Rohan Joshi    58
     2 Diya Shah      91

expl.en:
• CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT (CTAS) creates a new table with the columns of the query and copies the selected rows.
  • INSERT INTO ... SELECT copies rows from a query into an existing table (no VALUES keyword).
  • To copy only the structure, use a condition that is always false: CREATE TABLE t2 AS SELECT * FROM student WHERE 1 = 2;

title.en: SELECT columns, column alias and expression

code.en:
SELECT name, marks,
       marks * 100 / 150 AS percent,
       marks + 10 "New Marks"
FROM student;

Diya Shah      91 60.6666667       101
Karan Mehta    67 44.6666667        77
Isha Desai     74 49.3333333        84
Rohan Joshi    58 38.6666667        68

expl.en:
• SELECT picks columns; FROM names the table.
  • An expression such as marks * 100 / 150 is calculated for every row. It does not change the table.
  • Column alias: AS percent gives a heading (shown in capitals). With double quotes, "New Marks" keeps its case and spaces.

programs.out:
ROLLNO NAME        MARKS
------ ----------- -----

Aarav Patel Surat
Diya Shah   Vadodara

• WHERE filters rows. Only rows where the condition is TRUE are shown.
  • AND: both conditions must be true. OR: at least one must be true. NOT: reverses the condition.
  • Text comparison is case-sensitive: 'Surat' and 'SURAT' are different.

• Without DISTINCT, the value 'CE' appears once for every CE student.

title.en: DCL: create user and role, GRANT and REVOKE

programs.out:
User created.

Grant succeeded.

Grant succeeded.

Role created.

Grant succeeded.

Grant succeeded.

Revoke succeeded.

Grant succeeded.

expl.en:
• CREATE USER makes a new account (run as DBA/SYSTEM). CREATE SESSION is the system privilege needed to log in.
  • Object privileges (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) are given on a particular table with GRANT ... ON table TO user.
  • A role is a named group of privileges. Granting the role gives all of them at once, which makes management easy.
  • REVOKE takes a privilege back. Ravi can still SELECT and UPDATE (through the role) but can no longer INSERT.
  • WITH GRANT OPTION lets Meena grant SELECT to other users.

Ravi now uses the table as SELECT * FROM scott.student; (owner.table).

programs.out:
1 row created.

Commit complete.

3 rows deleted.

COUNT(*)
--------
       3

Rollback complete.

COUNT(*)
--------
       6

expl.en:
• INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are first kept in a transaction and are not yet permanent.
  • COMMIT makes them permanent and ends the transaction. Meera's row is now saved.
  • The DELETE removes 3 CE rows (count becomes 3), but ROLLBACK undoes everything after the last COMMIT, so the count is 6 again.
  • A normal exit from SQL*Plus commits; a crash or abnormal exit rolls back.

programs.out:
1 row created.

Savepoint created.

3 rows updated.

Savepoint created.

1 row deleted.

Rollback complete.

ROLLNO MARKS
------ -----
     1    87
     2    91
     3    72
     4    74
     5    63
     6    88

6 rows selected.

Rollback complete.

ROLLNO MARKS
------ -----
     1    82
     2    91
     3    67
     4    74
     5    58
     6    88

6 rows selected.

Commit complete.

expl.en:
• A SAVEPOINT marks a point inside a transaction.
  • ROLLBACK TO b undoes only the work done after b: the DELETE. Roll no. 5 is back, and the +5 update stays.
  • ROLLBACK TO a undoes the UPDATE too, so the marks return to their original values. The INSERT of roll no. 6 (before a) stays.
  • COMMIT saves what remains (the new row 6) and erases all savepoints.

programs.out:
1 row created.

Table created.

Rollback complete.

COUNT(*)
--------
       6

expl.en:
In Oracle, every DDL statement (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME) and DCL statement (GRANT, REVOKE) commits the current transaction automatically, before and after it runs.

So the INSERT was committed by CREATE TABLE, and the later ROLLBACK has nothing to undo: the count is still 6.

title.en: Data Item, Record, File and Database

terms.en: Defines a new table. DESC table_name shows its structure.
Copies structure and rows. WHERE 1 = 2 copies only the structure.
Changes structure: add, modify, drop or rename columns; rename the table.
DROP removes table + data. TRUNCATE removes all rows, keeps structure.
SQL*Plus command; shows Name, Null? and Type.
Adds rows. Use &var for substitution variables and / to run again.
Changes values. Without WHERE all rows are updated.
Removes rows. Can be rolled back before COMMIT.

items.f:
SELECT [DISTINCT] col1 [AS alias], ...
FROM table_name
[WHERE condition]
[GROUP BY columns]
[HAVING group_condition]
[ORDER BY columns [ASC|DESC]];

terms.en: Retrieves data. Execution order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY.
Run as DBA. A new user needs CREATE SESSION to log in.
WITH GRANT OPTION allows the user to pass the privilege on.
Takes back a privilege; cascades for object privileges.
A role is a named group of privileges.
DDL and DCL commit automatically in Oracle.

q.en: What is the difference between data and information?

a.en: Data is raw, unprocessed facts. Information is processed, meaningful data used for decision making.

q.en: What is metadata?

a.en: Data about data, e.g. table names, column names, data types and constraints.

q.en: What is a data dictionary?

a.en: A set of system tables (system catalog) where the DBMS stores all metadata. In Oracle it is read through views like USER_TABLES.

q.en: Define field, record and file.

a.en: Field: smallest named unit of data. Record: collection of related fields about one entity. File: collection of similar records.

q.en: What is a DBMS? Give examples.

a.en: Software to create, store, retrieve and manage a database. Examples: Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server, PostgreSQL.

q.en: What is an RDBMS?

a.en: A DBMS based on the relational model in which data is stored in related tables of rows and columns, e.g. Oracle.

q.en: Who proposed the relational model?

a.en: Dr. E. F. Codd of IBM, in 1970.

q.en: Name two disadvantages of the file system.

a.en: Data redundancy and data inconsistency (also difficult access, poor security, no concurrency).

q.en: Who is a DBA?

a.en: The Database Administrator: the person with central control who designs the schema, manages users and privileges, and takes backups.

q.en: What are the three levels of the ANSI/SPARC architecture?

a.en: External (view) level, conceptual (logical) level and internal (physical) level.

q.en: What is data independence?

a.en: The ability to change the schema at one level without changing the next higher level. It has two types: logical and physical.

q.en: What is the difference between a schema and an instance?

a.en: A schema is the structure/design of the database (changes rarely); an instance is the data stored at a particular moment (changes often).

q.en: What is a sub-schema?

a.en: A part of the schema visible to a particular user or application; created as a view in SQL.

q.en: What is SQL?

a.en: Structured Query Language: the standard non-procedural language for relational databases.

q.en: What is the difference between CHAR and VARCHAR2?

a.en: CHAR is fixed length and padded with spaces (max 2000 bytes); VARCHAR2 is variable length (max 4000 bytes).

q.en: What does NUMBER(7,2) mean?

a.en: 7 total digits with 2 after the decimal point; maximum value 99999.99.

q.en: Name the DDL commands.

a.en: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE and RENAME.

q.en: Name the DML commands.

a.en: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

q.en: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?

a.en: DELETE is DML, can use WHERE and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE is DDL, removes all rows and cannot be rolled back.

q.en: What is the difference between DROP and TRUNCATE?

a.en: DROP removes the table structure and data; TRUNCATE removes only the data and keeps the structure.

q.en: What happens if WHERE is omitted in UPDATE?

a.en: All rows of the table are updated.

q.en: What is the use of DISTINCT?

a.en: It removes duplicate rows from the result of a SELECT.

q.en: How do you see the structure of a table?

a.en: With the DESC (DESCRIBE) table_name command.

q.en: What is a substitution variable?

a.en: A variable written as &name in SQL*Plus; the user is asked to enter its value when the statement runs.

q.en: What is the use of GRANT and REVOKE?

a.en: GRANT gives privileges to users or roles; REVOKE takes them back.

q.en: What is a role?

a.en: A named group of privileges that can be granted to many users at once.

q.en: Difference between system and object privileges?

a.en: System privileges allow actions in the database (CREATE TABLE); object privileges allow actions on a specific object (SELECT on emp).

q.en: What is WITH GRANT OPTION?

a.en: It allows the user who receives an object privilege to grant it to other users.

q.en: What is a transaction?

a.en: A logical unit of work made of one or more SQL statements that is completed entirely or not at all.

q.en: Expand ACID.

a.en: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability.

q.en: What does COMMIT do?

a.en: It makes all changes of the current transaction permanent and ends the transaction.

q.en: What does ROLLBACK do?

a.en: It undoes all changes since the last COMMIT.

q.en: What is a SAVEPOINT?

a.en: A named marker inside a transaction; ROLLBACK TO savepoint undoes only the work after it.

q.en: Can a DROP TABLE be rolled back?

a.en: No. DDL commands commit automatically. (In Oracle 10g+ it can be restored with FLASHBACK TABLE ... TO BEFORE DROP.)
